# Space Skipping and Empty Volume Culling

Also called: Empty-space skipping, early ray termination, adaptive sampling

## Overview
Space skipping and empty volume culling are [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md) techniques in [image-order volume rendering](#11259-static-contiguous-image-based-partitioning.md) that reduce computational load by identifying and bypassing regions of the volume or ray path that do not contribute to the final image [S2][S4, S5]. What sets this family apart from its siblings is its primary focus on geometric or scalar-based determination of "visible" vs. "invisible" primitives (cells, voxels, or rays) before expensive integration occurs, whereas methods like [Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control](1791-early-termination-and-probabilistic-path-control.md) operate during the [ray-marching](#6739-ray-marching.md) process itself [G].

## Shared principles
The core mechanism shared by all acceleration methods is the reduction of work units (samples, voxels, or pixels) processed per frame while maintaining acceptable visual fidelity [G]. This is achieved through three primary strategies:
1. **Culling/Skipping:** Identifying regions of the volume or ray path that do not contribute to the final image (e.g., empty space, occluded voxels) and bypassing their evaluation [S2][S4, S5].
2. **Termination:** Halting the integration loop when the accumulated contribution becomes negligible (e.g., high opacity, low transmittance) [S1, S6, unofficial].
3. **Adaptation:** Varying the computational effort based on local scene complexity or global performance budgets [S1].

Mathematically, these methods modify the [standard front-to-back compositing](#1141-front-to-back-compositing-unpremultiplied.md) loop:
$$ C_{acc} = C_{acc} + C_{sample} \cdot \alpha_{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha_{acc}) $$
$$ \alpha_{acc} = \alpha_{acc} + \alpha_{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha_{acc}) $$
by introducing conditions that break the loop early, skip iterations, or reduce the number of $C_{sample}$ queries.

## Subtopics

### [Parallel Ray Casting with Segment Lists](2565-parallel-ray-casting-with-segment-lists.md)
[Parallel Ray Casting with Segment Lists](#2565-parallel-ray-casting-with-segment-lists.md) is a volume rendering acceleration method that combines [spatial decomposition](#9444-scene-representation-and-partitioning.md) of the image plane with ray-space culling via segment lists to skip empty space. It distributes rendering tasks across multiple processors (MPI ranks) and threads (OpenMP), calculating sampling points based on precomputed segment boundaries rather than iterating every voxel.

### [Visibility Culling](6226-visibility-culling.md)
[Visibility culling](#6226-visibility-culling.md) in volume rendering identifies and skips the processing of data regions or rays that do not contribute to the final image, thereby reducing computational load and memory bandwidth usage [G]. It differs from its siblings by focusing on the geometric or scalar-based determination of "visible" vs. "invisible" primitives (cells, voxels, or rays) before expensive integration or rasterization occurs, whereas methods like [Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control](1791-early-termination-and-probabilistic-path-control.md) operate during the ray-marching process itself [G].

### [Efficient Space Skipping & Adaptive Sampling of Unstructured Volumes Using H.W. Accel. Ray Tracing](8217-efficient-space-skipping-adaptive-sampling-of-unstructured-v.md)
This method enables interactive visualization of large unstructured volumes (e.g., from finite element simulations) by leveraging [hardware-accelerated ray tracing](#8936-ray-centric-and-hardware-accelerated-rendering.md) to accelerate acceleration structure traversal and point-in-element tests. It solves the bottleneck of traditional rasterization, which requires sorting 20–40 GB of unstructured elements front-to-back on every camera move, and addresses the limitation of existing space-skipping techniques that assume regular grids. It sets itself apart from siblings like [SparseLeap Ray-Casting with Occupancy Misses](9818-sparseleap-ray-casting-with-occupancy-misses.md) by explicitly combining empty space skipping with adaptive sampling on unstructured meshes using a KD-tree partitioning strategy, rather than relying solely on occupancy misses or segment lists.

### [SparseLeap Ray-Casting with Occupancy Misses](9818-sparseleap-ray-casting-with-occupancy-misses.md)
[SparseLeap](#5152-sparseleap.md) is a ray-guided volume rendering technique that separates [empty-space skipping](#1002-empty-space-skipping.md) metadata from volume data, using a ray segment list to process rays in discrete intervals. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like [Empty Space Skipping with Octree](1610-empty-space-skipping-with-octree.md) by delaying the determination of a brick's occupancy status until it is actually intersected by a view ray, thereby reducing depth complexity and avoiding unnecessary culling computations for occluded or out-of-frustum regions.

### Hierarchical Bounding Box Tree for Empty-Space Skipping
- **Definition:** A method for visualizing large-scale aerosols (smoke, fog, dust) by optimizing traditional [ray casting](#6080-ray-casting.md) to avoid sampling empty spaces and invalid voxels, reducing hardware load and improving speed [S1].
- **Steps:** Optimize and accelerate the traditional ray casting algorithm through the hierarchical bounding box tree [S1]. Combine an illumination model to enhance the color rendering of each voxel [S1].
- **Comparison:** Reduces unnecessary space debris to lower hardware load and improve rendering speed, meeting real-time rendering requirements for large-scale aerosols [S1].

### Surface Localization Acceleration
- **Definition:** Acceleration methods that localize the surface interface and concentrate samples only in relevant regions, effectively skipping empty space, because only 10-20% of evaluated samples have non-zero density [S2].
- **Steps:** Refine the sampling strategy to focus solely on the localized surface [S2].
- **Comparison:** Standard volumetric rendering is inefficient because it samples the entire ray; surface localization reduces the number of required MLP evaluations by skipping empty space [S2].

## Background
Standard volumetric rendering is inherently inefficient because it samples the entire ray, even though surface geometry occupies only a fraction of the 3D space. As observed by Piala et al. [PC21] and Hu et al. [HLC∗ 22], only around 10 to 20% of the evaluated samples have non-zero density and actually contribute to the final image [S2]. To address this, acceleration methods aim to localize the surface interface and concentrate samples only in these relevant regions, effectively skipping empty space [S2]. Existing approaches generally fall into four categories based on how they define this region of interest: (1) using sparse data structures [SSC22], (2) leveraging depth oracles [NSP∗ 21,LPX∗ 22], (3) guiding sampling via [Signed Distance Fields](#1466-signed-distance-fields-sdf.md) [SZZ∗ 22,WRB∗ 23] or density estimates [HLC∗ 22], and (4) employing learned sampling networks [PC21,KNL∗ 22] [S2].

For large-scale aerosol visualization (smoke, fog, dust), traditional ray casting algorithms suffer from low efficiency, slow speed, and large resource consumption [S1]. A method proposed in [S1] optimizes the algorithm through a hierarchical bounding box tree to avoid sampling empty spaces and invalid voxels, combining this with an illumination model to enhance color rendering.
